newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina united in protest of Brazil import rules.
newsitem.headline: Argentina united in protest of Brazil import rules.

text.p: Argentine industry and government united on Monday in a chorus of protest against new Brazilian import rules as Economy Minister Roque Fernandez prepared an emergency trip to argue against the moves.

"Brazil has acted badly, because it should have consulted before taking any decisive measure which damages the interests of its neighbors," Argentine Deputy Foreign Minister Andres Cisneros told local radio.

Still, Cisneros -- who will accompany Fernandez to Brasilia on Tuesday -- said Argentina was not contemplating any reprisals against Brazil's unexpected decision last week to slap restrictions on short-term financing for imports.

Brazil's central bank ruled that most Brazilian importers with financing of less than 360 days will have to take out foreign exchange contracts on the day they receive their goods from customs. The new procedure, designed to make short-term financing more difficult to arrange for buyers of foreign goods, should help slim Brazil's swollen trade deficit.

Argentina, which last year recorded a $1.0 billion trade surplus exporting $6.5 billion of goods to its neighbor, wants Brazil to exclude its partners in the Mercosur customs union from the new restrictions.
The head of Argentina's Chamber of Exporters, Enrique Mantilla, said Brazil's move would damage the image of Mercosur, which only began to operate as a customs union in January 1995.
"What credibility will Mercosur have if it violates its own agreements?" said Mantilla, accusing the Brazilians of defying Mercosur's recent pact with Chile, which forbade new trade restrictions.
In addition to Argentina and Brazil, Mercosur is comprised of Uruguay and Paraguay, while Chile is an associate member.

All of Brazil's regional partners have complained about the new rules. Brazil has said it will evaluate their requests for exemptions on a bilateral basis. Argentina is urging Brazil to exempt all Mercosur countries.

"Brazil has to decide whether if is going to fight alone against the whole world or if it needs the help of its partners in Mercosur," Mantilla said. He said Brazil's decision also violated the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT).

Under Secretary for Food Susana Merlo speculated that Brazil would reverse its decision, under pressure not only from Argentina as well as complaints of other countries to the World Trade Organization.
President Carlos Menem played down the dispute.

"We are going to solve this. I am sure we will reach an understanding," he said on a television chat show, adding that he could speak personally to Brazil's President Henrique Fernando Cardoso about the matter "if it were necessary."
Menem is due to visit Brazil in late April.
The latest spat between Mercosur's two biggest economies comes on top of a bitter dispute over Brazilian incentives encouraging foreign car companies to build factories in its impoverished northeast.
Argentina exports large quantities of wheat and other foods to Brazil, as well as manufactured goods.
